01-intro: Today is all about crazy game mashups, what they have to do with reverse engineering, what role AI plays – and why this could get pretty uncomfortable for software companies.
My timeline is full of videos right now in which different video games and their game mechanics are mixed together.
The pictures below show some examples: characters, game worlds and the way you move, build or fight are combined in new ways.
Behind them are different technical approaches, including reverse engineering – examining finished software to understand how it works.
Mario in Elden Ring, for example, is based on a decompilation of Super Mario 64, according to its project description – exactly this kind of look inside a game.
What's new is the speed: AI can massively accelerate this laborious analysis and programming work – which is why mashups like these are popping up almost every week.
I'll show you how this works behind the next door.
02-compile: A human writes source code, for example in C: a programming language that people can read and understand well.
The compiler translates it into machine language – shown here as zeros and ones, which the computer can work with, but we humans hardly can.
Games and commercial programs are usually shipped only as machine code – the readable source code stays with the vendor.
That's exactly what protected software for a long time: figuring out how it works from machine code was tedious – and made rebuilding it expensive.
Now I'll jump on the decompiler button and show you the way back.
03-decompile-cleanroom: Now we go from machine language back to readable code.
This is called decompiling – one method of reverse engineering.
This was possible before – but look at the result: no comments, no meaningful names. Understanding this code was difficult, time-consuming and expensive.
This is where AI comes in: it recognizes what the code does, suggests understandable names and explains it – work that used to take a lot of expert time.
For the game mashups, this means: once game mechanics are understood – such as a character's jumping or fighting – they can be built into another game.
Sometimes two running games are connected, too; AI can help develop the analysis and connection code needed for that faster.
But there's another way: you observe what a program does and describe its features.
In a classic clean-room implementation, one team documents these features.
Another team then writes its own code from that description, without knowing the original code.
Here, too, AI can help reprogram the described features – whether the separation is still clean, though, is an open question.
And now it gets serious: this doesn't just affect video games, but also the software we work with every day.
04-artcraft-outlook: This is ArtCraft: according to media reports, a developer used AI to publish rebuilds of seven Adobe programs within a few weeks – including Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere.
PhotoCraft shows how similar such a rebuild already looks – free and open source, while Adobe sells its programs as a monthly subscription.
According to the developers, these are clean-room implementations: public descriptions and observed behavior instead of Adobe's original code.
According to the project, PhotoCraft is not yet a full replacement for professional Photoshop work.
Still, the vendors are unlikely to be happy about it: what was developed over decades and is paid for by subscription can suddenly be rebuilt in weeks.
And this is exactly where it gets tricky: according to the project's own documentation, files from an installed Photoshop version were examined as well – does that still count as a clean room?
Rebuilding features isn't automatically copyright infringement – but trademarks, patents and license terms are separate issues.
There's already a fierce debate about AI and copyright – including what AI models may learn from other people's software.
How courts would judge AI rebuilds like these is still an open question.
For us, this means: software is becoming more interchangeable – the value lies more and more in ideas, experience and good results.
AI makes rebuilding software easier than ever – the big question is: how will software companies protect what makes them unique in the future?
